name: The Cuban Lignum Vitae

location.address: Key West Tropical Forest & Botanical Garden, 5210 College Road, Stock Island, Key West, FL 33040 (Boardwalk section)

access: Paid admission (nominal fee; free for Key West/Monroe County locals on the first Sunday of every month); open daily. Stands within the garden's public grounds on the Boardwalk.
transport: No direct city bus to the garden gate; the Lower Keys Shuttle (city of Key West) stops at US 1 / College Road on Stock Island, a short walk away. By car, about 4 km / 10 minutes from Old Town Key West, with on-site parking.
verify_notes: Florida (State) Champion Guaiacum officinale, on the garden's Boardwalk. Two independent sources agree: the garden's own 2024 post-Hurricane-Irma status page lists it 'OK' (undamaged, one of the few champions the storm spared), and Wikipedia's article on the garden (last edited 2026-08-23) independently lists it as Florida Champion. No live snapshot newer than 2024-07-21 exists in the Wayback CDX index as of 2026-09-25 (checked directly), and the garden's own site returns a bot-challenge to automated fetches, so 2024 is the newest status available; nothing found since suggests a change. No age or girth published anywhere found. Lignum vitae (ironwood) is one of the densest, slowest-growing timbers in the world, which is itself the reason a specimen this size holds a state title; worth a line for the writer. Garden founded 1936 as a WPA hardwood-hammock project (ArbNet), but no source ties this specific tree to that planting date, so no age should be inferred from it.

verify_notes: Florida Champion Barringtonia asiatica, on the Boardwalk. Two independent sources agree: garden's own 2024 post-Irma status page lists it 'OK', Wikipedia's garden article (edited 2026-08-23) independently lists it as Florida Champion. Species is native to Indo-Pacific shorelines, not Florida; its large white-and-pink powderpuff flowers open at night and its fibrous, angular fruit (the 'box fruit' or fish-poison fruit, used traditionally to stun fish) floats and disperses by sea, which is a good visual/story hook. The garden's own 2024 post-Hurricane-Irma status page (Sept 2017 storm) is explicit and in its own words: 'Wild Dilly (West Loop) - Partially down but still alive', listed as 'Former National Champion | Damaged' in its photo captions. The Key West Botanical Garden Society's own 2017 damage report to the American Public Gardens Association independently corroborates that this hurricane badly hit the garden's specimen trees generally (major wind damage across the grounds, most of the 81-year-old canopy affected). Wikipedia's garden article, last edited 2026-08-23, by contrast lists it plainly as a current 'National Champion' with no damage noted, which may mean it has recovered enough to keep the title, or may simply be an incomplete update; no fresher primary-source status than the 2024 garden page was found (checked Wayback CDX through today, no capture newer than 2024-07-21; the live site blocks automated fetches with a bot-challenge). Write it honestly as storm-damaged but alive, per the source's own words, rather than as a pristine champion. No age or girth found.
